title: Why Ryup has no snooze button: the backend-tuned retry ladder behind every alarm
excerpt: Ryup has no snooze, on purpose. Instead, an unanswered alarm climbs a retry ladder whose numbers live on our backend, run by Android's AlarmManager and Apple's AlarmKit in two very different ways.
content:
Almost every alarm clock ever made has a snooze button. Ryup does not, and that is not an oversight. Our wake-up design document says it in bold: no snooze button, anywhere, in any state.

But "no snooze" does not mean "rings once and gives up". An alarm that you sleep through still has to try again. So instead of snooze, every Ryup alarm climbs a short **retry ladder**: ring, wait, ring again, wait, ring a last time. The numbers on that ladder (how long a ring lasts, how long the gap is, how many rungs there are) live on our backend, so we can tune them without shipping a new app.

This post explains how that ladder works, from the admin screen where a number is changed, through a Go server and a Flutter app, down to two very different native alarm systems: Android's `AlarmManager` and Apple's AlarmKit. It also covers the bugs we hit, and the places where it is still not perfect.

If you have not read it yet, our earlier post on [building a reliable alarm on iOS and Android](/blog/reliable-alarm-ios-alarmkit-android-exact-alarms) covers the basics of getting a phone to ring at all. This one starts where that one stops: what happens when nobody answers.

### A short glossary

- **Retry ladder:** our name for the sequence of rings in one morning. The first ring plus up to two retries.
- **Attempt:** one rung of the ladder. One ring, and the activity that may follow it.
- **Activity:** the small task Ryup asks you to do out loud to turn the alarm off, such as reading a short passage.
- **Backend:** our server, written in Go, which stores accounts and settings. The app talks to it over the internet.
- **Remote config:** settings the app downloads from the backend instead of having them built in, so they can change without an app update.
- **Native code:** code written in the phone's own languages (Kotlin on Android, Swift on iPhone), as opposed to our shared Flutter code in Dart.
- **AlarmManager:** Android's built-in service for running something at an exact time.
- **AlarmKit:** Apple's alarm system for apps, added in iOS 26. It rings like the built-in Clock app.
- **Pigeon:** a code generator that writes the "bridge" between Flutter and native code from one shared definition, so both sides agree on every message.

## Why there is no snooze

Snooze trains a habit: hear the alarm, press a button, go back to sleep. Ryup exists to break that habit. The only way to silence a Ryup alarm is to start the activity, or to finish it.

We wanted that rule to survive future changes, including ones made in a hurry. So it is not just written in a design document. It is a test that runs on every build, for every attempt on the ladder:

```dart
testWidgets('there is never a snooze button - ${attempt.name}', (
  WidgetTester tester,
) async {
  await pumpFiring(tester, attempt: attempt);
  expect(find.textContaining('nooze'), findsNothing);
});
```

The test searches the ringing screen for "nooze", so "Snooze", "snooze" and "Snoozed" all fail it. If anyone ever adds the button, the build goes red.

There was one more temptation. Apple's AlarmKit comes with its own snooze, built into the system alert. We chose not to use it, for three reasons we wrote down at the time:

1. It only works when the user **taps** it. Our whole design depends on what happens when nobody taps anything.
2. The alert has room for one extra button, and we had already given that button to "Open Ryup".
3. It needs an extra app component (a widget extension) that the rest of the app did not need.

### "No snooze" is not "no escape"

A wake-up app that cannot be stopped is a broken app. Two exits always exist:

- A **Close** control is there from the very first ring. It does not cancel the morning, it just lets you leave the screen.
- Once the retries are used up, a **press-and-hold "give up for today"** ends the morning on purpose.

Holding the button, instead of tapping it, makes giving up a decision rather than a reflex.

## The retry ladder, step by step

A Ryup morning is made of up to three attempts: the first ring, then up to two retries.

![Diagram: one Ryup morning as a ladder of three rings. Each unanswered ring lasts up to 90 seconds, then the phone waits 5 minutes and rings again. Tapping in opens a 10 minute activity window. After the third failed ring the morning is marked missed.](/blog/ryup/08-retry-ladder.svg)

An attempt can fail in two different ways:

1. **The ring goes unanswered.** You sleep through it.
2. **You tap in but never finish.** You start the activity, then put the phone down and drift off again.

Both draw from the same budget. That was a deliberate choice. If tapping in and walking away did not cost an attempt, it would be a snooze button with extra steps.

When an attempt fails and there are retries left, the phone waits and rings again. When the last one fails, the morning is recorded as **missed**, and the app shows a "you missed this morning" page, exactly once.

Here are the production numbers:

| Setting | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ring timeout | 90 seconds | How long one unanswered ring lasts (Android) |
| Retry wait | 5 minutes | The gap before the next ring |
| Retry count | 2 | Retries after the first ring, so 3 rings in total |
| Activity window | 10 minutes | How long you have to finish once you have tapped in |
| Race buffer | 10 seconds | Extra slack on top of the window, explained below |

### The window counts from your last action

The activity window used to start when you tapped in. That turned out to be wrong. A person who spoke slowly, or paused to think, could be sent to the "missed" page in the middle of a sentence.

The fix was to measure the window from your **last real action**, not from the moment you started. Every time the app reports progress, the deadline moves. A person working steadily never gets near it, however long their morning runs. Only someone who has genuinely stopped runs out of time.

The **race buffer** exists for the moment the deadline and your last tap land almost together. Without it, the phone could decide "missed" a few milliseconds before it heard about the answer you just gave. Ten seconds of slack removes that race.

### Why the window grew from 5 to 10 minutes

On 2026-09-13 a Ryup morning grew from one activity to between two and four. The old 5-minute window was still fine for anyone working steadily, because it resets on every action. But it no longer covered someone who stopped halfway and came back. So we raised it to 10 minutes.

That change is the reason this whole post exists. It was a one-number change, and we made it without an app release, because the number lives on the backend.

## Why the numbers live on the backend

Alarm timings are product decisions, and product decisions change. If the numbers were built into the app, every change would mean a new release, a store review, and days or weeks before most phones updated.

So the ladder's numbers are part of a backend setting we call the **pre-alarm config**: everything the phone needs to know before an alarm goes off.

### Versions, never edits

The config lives in a Postgres table where rows are **never edited**. Changing a number means creating a new version, then activating it. A special database index (a partial unique index) allows only one row to be active at a time.

This has a quiet benefit. When someone asks "what were the alarm timings on the morning of the 12th?", there is an exact answer, because the row that was active then still exists, unchanged. Version names say what changed, for example `v3-shorter-read-minimums`, rather than just "v3".

Our admin panel groups these numbers under a heading called **Ringing**: "How long the alarm sounds, and what happens when nobody answers." The admin can create a version, see a diff against the active one, and activate it. There is no "edit" button, by design.

### Validation before anything goes live

A config cannot be activated unless it passes a set of checks. Every timing must be greater than zero, and that includes the retry count: the backend refuses a config that would turn retries off entirely.

There is also a "window-fit" check. It works out the longest recording a morning could ask for, adds the race buffer, and refuses any config where that does not fit inside the activity window. A config that would make a morning impossible to finish in time cannot go live.

### The server never lets a config problem break an alarm

The Go service keeps the active config in memory and re-reads it from the database every 60 seconds. If that read fails, it falls back in three steps:

1. **The active database row**, the normal case.
2. **The last copy that loaded and validated successfully**, held in memory.
3. **Compiled-in defaults**, the numbers built into the server itself.

Each step down is logged loudly, but the person asking never sees an error. The comment above that code puts it in one line: *"A person's alarm must not depend on this table being healthy."*

## The journey from the backend to the phone

![Diagram: how an alarm setting travels. An admin activates a new config version; the Go server loads it with fallbacks to last-known-good and defaults; the app fetches it on start and resume, stores it with no expiry, and passes it to Android SharedPreferences or iOS UserDefaults, where the alarm code reads it when it rings.](/blog/ryup/08-config-journey.svg)

The app fetches the config from one signed-in endpoint, `GET /v1/me/pre-alarm`. The part the retry ladder uses looks like this:

```json
{
  "timing": {
    "ring_timeout_seconds": 90,
    "activity_window_seconds": 600,
    "race_buffer_seconds": 10,
    "retry_wait_seconds": 300,
    "retry_count": 2
  },
  "fetched_at": "2026-10-20T06:00:00Z",
  "refresh_after_seconds": 86400
}
```

The real response carries more than this (recording rules and a few other morning settings), but those belong to a different post.

### A config that never expires

Notice what is missing: an expiry date. `refresh_after_seconds` tells the phone when to come back for a newer copy. It does **not** tell the phone when to stop trusting the old one.

That was the most important design decision in the whole pipeline, and the code comment explains it better than we can:

> There is no expiry, deliberately: a phone that has been on a plane, in a dead zone, or had background refresh off for four days holds an old copy, and if old meant unusable we would have made an alarm fail in order to protect a configuration value. Nothing in this response may ever be a reason an alarm does not ring properly.

### No network call at 6 AM

The app refreshes the config when it starts and every time it comes back to the foreground. There is no background timer. If a refresh fails, the old copy stays. The stored copy lives in the app's local database, as a single row.

When the alarm code needs the numbers, it reads them in a fixed order:

1. **A special "fast alarms" test build wins outright.** It shrinks the ladder (15-second rings, 20-second waits, a 4-minute window) so we can walk a whole three-ring morning by hand in about a minute and a half instead of a quarter of an hour.
2. **Then the last copy the backend sent.**
3. **Then built-in defaults**, for a phone that has never managed to fetch, such as a brand-new install that went offline straight away.

None of these steps touches the network. An alarm books correctly with the phone in aeroplane mode.

### Handing the numbers to native code

The ladder is not run by Flutter. It is run by native code, because native code is what wakes up when the alarm fires, even if the app is closed. So the Flutter side hands the numbers down through a Pigeon bridge, in a message called `AlarmRetryConfig`:

- **Android** stores it as JSON in `SharedPreferences`, Android's small key-value store.
- **iPhone** stores it in `UserDefaults`, Apple's equivalent.

From here on, the two platforms behave very differently.

## Android: the phone runs the ladder itself

On Android, every ring and every retry is booked with `AlarmManager.setAlarmClock`. We chose it over the other exact-alarm methods because it is the one Android treats as a real, user-visible alarm, which keeps it working through Doze (Android's deep battery-saving sleep).

When a ring fires, a **foreground service** starts playing the sound. A foreground service is a piece of the app that Android promises not to kill while it shows a notification. The service also starts a 90-second timer. If nobody answers before it runs out, the attempt has failed.

Every failed attempt, whichever way it failed, goes through one function, with one decision in it:

```kotlin
fun handleAttemptFailed(context: Context, alarmId: Long) {
    val attempt = AlarmStore.getActiveAttempt(context, alarmId) ?: return
    val config = AlarmStore.getRetryConfig(context)
    val nextAttemptNumber = attempt.attemptNumber + 1
    // ...
    if (nextAttemptNumber > 1 + config.maxRetries) {
        AlarmStore.clearActiveAttempt(context, alarmId)
        AlarmStore.setMissedAlarm(context, alarmId)
        AlarmHostApiImpl.notifyDartOfMissIfAlive(context, alarmId)
        return
    }
    scheduleRetry(
        context,
        AlarmSchedule(
            alarmId = attempt.alarmId,
            triggerAtEpochMillis = System.currentTimeMillis() + config.retryWaitMillis,
            label = attempt.label,
            volumeRampEnabled = attempt.volumeRampEnabled,
            toneAssetPath = attempt.toneAssetPath,
            attemptNumber = nextAttemptNumber,
            // ...
        ),
    )
    // ...
}
```

A few details in there each came from a real problem:

- **The config is read fresh every time.** Android reads the stored numbers at the moment it needs them, so whatever the app last handed down applies to the next ring.
- **A retry keeps the alarm's label, tone and fade-in.** Your 6:05 retry sounds like your 6:00 alarm, not like a generic beep.
- **The next ring is timed from now, not from the plan.** A retry waits the full 5 minutes from the moment the previous attempt failed.

### The bug that made retries live on their own

Early on, opening the app at 6:02 could silently delete the 6:05 retry. When the app starts, it rebuilds the whole alarm schedule from your saved alarms, to make sure the phone and the app agree. That rebuild cleared everything it did not recognise, and a pending retry was not one of your saved alarms.

We confirmed it before fixing it: a retry due at 19:00:35 was gone after a cold start at 19:00:28. The fix gives retries their own storage and their own action name in the alarm system, so the schedule rebuild cannot touch them. That rule (retries live outside the schedule) is now one of the written rules every alarm change has to respect.

### Gentle wake-up

On Android, each alarm can fade in. The sound starts at 15% volume and rises in a straight line to full volume over 30 seconds, in half-second steps. It is on by default, and you can turn it off per alarm. A retry inherits the setting of the attempt that failed.

Nothing gets louder between attempts. The third ring sounds like the first.

### What Android does not do

The activity deadline (the 10-minute window) uses a different method, `setExactAndAllowWhileIdle`, instead of `setAlarmClock`. That is deliberate. It is an invisible check, not a real alarm, and `setAlarmClock` would show a misleading "next alarm" time on the status bar and lock screen, as if it were your real wake-up. The cost is that it is not fully protected from Doze. We accept that, because you have just unlocked the phone to tap in, so it is nowhere near deep sleep at that moment.

The 90-second timer lives inside the running app. If someone swipes the app away while it is ringing, that timer goes with it, and no retry is booked. We know about this one and have written it down.

## iPhone: one ring at a time, booked when you dismiss it

On iPhone, Ryup uses AlarmKit, which needs iOS 26.1 or later. There is no fallback to ordinary notifications. AlarmKit gives us a real system alarm, but it also takes away a lot of control, and we measured exactly how much on a real iPhone 16 running iOS 26.6:

- It rings through Silent mode at full volume.
- An ignored alarm kept ringing for at least 5 minutes 22 seconds and never stopped on its own during the test.
- It rings after the app has been force-killed, and after a reboot while the phone is still locked.
- Pressing the side button, a volume button or touching the screen silences it for good, **and tells the app nothing**.
- The alert does not open the app.

That changes what "ring timeout" means. On Android, we stop the sound after 90 seconds. On iPhone, the system owns the sound, and an ignored alarm ends whenever iOS decides. Our notes put that somewhere between 6 and 30 minutes.

### Version one: book every ring in advance

The first iPhone design booked all three rings ahead of time, at the planned times. On a real device, that went badly. A first ring that nobody touched was still alerting more than 5 minutes later, when the second one fired. AlarmKit alerts **stack, they do not queue**, so a sleeping person could end up with a pile of alerts all ringing at once.

### Version two: reserve one, book the next on dismissal

The design we ship now is simple to state: **only one ring of a morning is ever booked with the system at a time**.

- While one of the morning's rings is alerting, nothing new is booked.
- Otherwise, only the earliest upcoming ring is booked.
- When you dismiss a ring, an App Intent (Apple's way of letting a system button run a small piece of your app's code) calls `ringDismissed`, which times the remaining rings from that moment and books the next one.

```swift
let start = now.addingTimeInterval(Double(morning.config.retryWaitMillis) / 1000)
let spacing = Double(morning.attemptSpacingMillis) / 1000
morning.bookings = remaining
  .sorted { $0.attempt < $1.attempt }
  .enumerated()
  .map { offset, booking in
    BookingRecord(
      attempt: booking.attempt,
      kind: booking.kind,
      fireAtEpochMillis: Int64(
        start.addingTimeInterval(Double(offset) * spacing).timeIntervalSince1970 * 1000)
    )
  }
```

So the 5-minute gap is measured from when you sent the last ring away, not from when it was planned. Dismissing a ring instantly still gets you the full 5 minutes, which is exactly the kind of thing a test should pin down. One of our iOS tests is named, literally, `testAnImmediateDismissalStillWaitsTheFullRetryGap`.

There is one more rule. If an activity is running, a stray dismissal of an old ring is ignored. Otherwise, sending away a ring you no longer need could re-time the morning underneath the activity you are in the middle of.

![Diagram: Android and iPhone side by side. On Android, a 90 second timer ends an unanswered ring and the phone books the next ring 5 minutes later with setAlarmClock. On iPhone, one ring is booked at a time; when the user dismisses it, an App Intent books the next ring 5 minutes after the dismissal.](/blog/ryup/08-android-vs-ios.svg)

### Each iPhone morning keeps its own numbers

On iPhone, the config is copied into each planned morning when it is scheduled. When the schedule is rebuilt, mornings that are already under way keep the numbers they started with, and only future mornings get the new ones. A morning never changes its rules halfway through.

### The limits we work inside

Because the ring does not open the app, a repeating alarm on iPhone cannot rely on the app to book tomorrow's ring. So Ryup books up to 15 upcoming occurrences of each repeating alarm in advance. It also keeps the total under a budget of 600 bookings, spread fairly across your alarms, so one alarm can never crowd out another.

There is a known hole. Between a reboot and the first time the phone is unlocked, the App Intent that books the next ring does not run. A morning in that state gets one ring instead of three. It is tracked as an open issue, not hidden.

There is also no fade-in on iPhone. AlarmKit does not give apps volume control, so the per-alarm "gentle wake-up" setting only affects Android.

## Same numbers, different meanings

The backend sends one config. Each platform reads it in its own way:

| Setting | Android | iPhone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ring timeout (90 s) | Stops the sound and fails the attempt | Not applied; the system ends an ignored alarm |
| Retry wait (5 min) | From the moment the attempt failed | From the moment the ring was dismissed |
| Retry count (2) | Checked in `handleAttemptFailed` | Planned into each morning's bookings |
| Activity window (10 min) | Exact background check, moved on every action | Same rule, moved on every action |
| Config changes | Read fresh at every ring | Copied into each morning when it is planned |
| Fade-in | 15% to full over 30 s, per alarm | Not available |

We think this table is the most useful thing in the post. The same five numbers produce two different behaviours, and both are correct for their platform. Writing the table down is what stopped us from "fixing" one platform to match the other.

## Retrying requests is a different problem

"Retry" also shows up in Ryup's networking code, and it is worth seeing how different the rules are.

When a request to our backend fails because the server is busy, the app tries again, but only a little: at most three attempts, starting at about one second and doubling, with a little random "jitter" so that many phones do not retry at the same instant. The comment sets the expectation: at most about 4.5 seconds, about 1.2 seconds in the ordinary case.

Uploading your morning's recordings is stricter still. If the server says a recording is missing, the app re-sends once. The code comment says it in five words: "One retry, not a loop."

The difference is the point. An alarm retry is a product feature: it exists to wake a person up, so it is patient and measured in minutes. A network retry protects a server: it has to be short and polite, or thousands of phones retrying together become the outage.

## How we test a ladder that takes a quarter of an hour

A real morning with every ring ignored takes about 14 and a half minutes on Android: three 90-second rings and two 5-minute gaps. Nobody can test that by hand twenty times a day. So we test it at four levels:

1. **Dart unit tests** check which source of numbers wins (fast build, then backend copy, then defaults) and that the snooze button never appears.
2. **Kotlin tests**, run with Robolectric (a tool that runs Android code on a laptop without a phone), cover the retry, the cap, the missed morning, and that a retry keeps its fade-in.
3. **Swift tests** for the iPhone scheduler, including `testAWholeMorningNeverHoldsMoreThanOneRingAtATime` and `testAnIgnoredMorningRunsOutRatherThanRingingForever`.
4. **Real devices**, using the fast build to walk a whole morning in about a minute and a half, and then once more with production timings, which we did on the iPhone 16.

The fast build taught us a lesson of its own. We first shrank every timer by roughly the same amount, which made the debug activity window 30 seconds long. But the debug activity itself took about a minute. So a debug build could not be finished in time **at all**, and it sent the person testing to the "missed" page mid-activity. It looked exactly like a product bug.

The fix was to scale each timer against the thing it times, not by one blanket factor. The rule we wrote down: a compressed build should behave like production, only faster. It should never behave differently.

## What we would still improve

Being honest about the gaps is part of the design:

- **A config change reaches the alarm code later than it could.** The app hands the numbers to native code once per launch. A new version downloaded during that launch is stored straight away, but it only reaches the alarm code the next time the app starts. Our admin panel says a change takes effect "within about a minute", which is true for the server, not yet for every phone. Today the backend and the built-in defaults hold the same numbers, so nobody is affected, but it is the next thing to fix.
- **A reboot before first unlock** gives an iPhone morning one ring instead of three.
- **Swiping the app away mid-ring** on Android cancels that ring's timeout, so no retry is booked.
- **Force Stop** on Android cancels every alarm. That is how Android works, and no app can get around it.

## What we learned

1. **Write the product rule as a test.** "No snooze" is one line of test code, and it will outlive every one of us remembering why.
2. **Settings that can break an alarm must never expire.** Old numbers are better than no alarm.
3. **Version settings, never edit them.** Being able to say exactly what was active on any morning is worth the extra table rows.
4. **Let each platform do it its own way.** Android lets us control the ring. iPhone does not. One shared config, two honest implementations, and a table that says how they differ.
5. **Test on a real phone.** The stacked-alerts problem on iPhone and the deleted retry on Android were both found by using the app, not by the test suite. The tests now guard against both.

Ryup is on [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.ryup_app), free, and the iPhone version is coming soon. If you build alarm or reminder features yourself, we hope the retry ladder saves you a few of the mornings it cost us.

For more on how Ryup is built, read how we [structured the Flutter app](/blog/flutter-app-architecture-riverpod-ios-android) and how the [Go backend](/blog/go-backend-gin-postgres-for-a-mobile-app) that serves this config is put together.
